title: Capitalize the Title
description:
You are given a string `title` consisting of one or more words separated by a single space, where each word consists of English letters. Capitalize the string by applying the following rules:
- If the length of the word is 1 or 2 letters, change all letters to lowercase.
- Otherwise, change the first letter to uppercase and the remaining letters to lowercase.

Return the capitalized `title`.
constraints: title consists of words separated by a single space without leading or trailing spaces.
Each word consists of English letters.
hints: Split the title by spaces, format each word based on its length, and join them back with a single space.

test_cases.explanation: Since all the words have length greater than 2 except 'tHe', 'capiTalIze' becomes 'Capitalize', 'tHe' has length 3 so it becomes 'The', and 'titLe' becomes 'Title'.
The word 'of' has length 2 so it is changed to lowercase 'of'. Other words have length > 2 and their first letter is capitalized.

title: Check if Numbers Are Ascending in a Sentence
description:
A sentence is a list of tokens separated by a single space with no leading or trailing spaces. Every token is either a positive integer consisting of digits 0-9 without leading zeros, or a word consisting of lowercase English letters.

Given a string `s` representing a sentence, return `true` if all the numbers in `s` are strictly increasing from left to right, or `false` otherwise.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters, spaces, and digits from 0 to 9.
The number of tokens in s is between 2 and 100.
Tokens are separated by a single space.
There is at least two numbers in s.
hints: Extract all numeric tokens in order, and check whether each number is strictly greater than the preceding one.

inputs.s: 1 box has 3 blue 4 red 6 green and 12 yellow marbles

test_cases.explanation: The numbers in the sentence are 1, 3, 4, 6, 12, which are strictly increasing.
The numbers are 5, 5, which are not strictly increasing (equal values).

inputs.s: sunset comes at 7 31 pm walk at 7 34 pm

title: Percentage of Letter in String
description: Given a string `s` and a character `letter`, return the percentage of characters in `s` that equal `letter` rounded down to the nearest whole percent.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
letter is a single lowercase English letter.
hints: Count occurrences of letter, multiply by 100, and perform integer division by the length of s.

test_cases.explanation: The letter 'o' appears 2 times in 'foobar' (length 6). (2 / 6) * 100 = 33.33%, which rounds down to 33.
The letter 'k' does not appear in 'jjjj', so the percentage is 0%.

title: Strong Password Checker II
description:
A password is said to be strong if it satisfies all the following criteria:
- It has at least 8 characters.
- It contains at least one lowercase letter.
- It contains at least one uppercase letter.
- It contains at least one digit.
- It contains at least one special character from: `!@#$%^&*()-+`.
- It does not contain 2 of the same character in adjacent positions.

Given a string `password`, return `true` if it is a strong password, or `false` otherwise.
constraints: password consists of English letters, digits, and special characters '!@#$%^&*()-+'.
hints: Check each of the 6 conditions independently with a single pass over the password string.

test_cases.explanation: The password has length 14, contains uppercase, lowercase, digit, special character '!', and no two adjacent identical characters.
The password contains adjacent identical characters '--', so it is not strong.

title: Check if Matrix Is X-Matrix
description:
A square 2D matrix `grid` of size `n x n` is called an X-Matrix if both of the following conditions hold:
- All the elements in the diagonals of the matrix are non-zero.
- All other elements are 0.

Return `true` if `grid` is an X-Matrix, and `false` otherwise.
hints: An element grid[i][j] is on a diagonal if i == j or i + j == n - 1.

test_cases.explanation: Elements on diagonals are all non-zero, and all off-diagonal elements are 0.
grid[0][1] == 7 is not on a diagonal, and grid[2][2] == 0 is on a diagonal, violating both conditions.

title: Count Asterisks
description:
You are given a string `s`, where every two consecutive vertical bars `'|'` are grouped into a pair. In other words, the 1st and 2nd `'|'` make a pair, the 3rd and 4th make a pair, and so on.

Return the number of asterisks `'*'` in `s`, excluding each `'*'` between each pair of `'|'`.

Note that each `'|'` will belong to exactly one pair.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters, vertical bars '|', and asterisks '*'.
s has an even number of '|'.
hints: Maintain a boolean flag tracking whether you are currently inside a pair of bars.

test_cases.explanation: The asterisks between the first pair of bars and the second pair are excluded. The remaining asterisks outside pairs are 2 (in 'c**o').
There are no vertical bars and no asterisks, so output is 0.

title: First Letter to Appear Twice
description:
Given a string `s` consisting of lowercase English letters, return the first letter to appear twice.

Note that a letter `a` appears twice before another letter `b` if the second occurrence of `a` is before the second occurrence of `b`.

`s` will contain at least one letter that appears more than once.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
s has at least one repeated letter.
hints: Iterate through the string with a set of visited characters. The first character you see already in the set is the answer.

test_cases.explanation: The letter 'c' is the first to appear twice, as its second occurrence is at index 3.
The letter 'd' is the only letter that appears twice.

title: Minimum Cuts to Divide a Circle
description:
A valid cut in a circle can be a line that touches two points on the edge and passes through the center (diameter), or a straight segment connecting the center to the edge (radius).

Given the integer `n`, return the minimum number of cuts needed to divide a circle into `n` equal slices.
hints: If n is 1, no cuts are needed.
If n is even, each diameter cut creates 2 slices, so n / 2 cuts are needed.
If n is odd, each slice needs its own radius cut from the center, so n cuts are needed.

test_cases.explanation: Cutting the circle 2 times through the center creates 4 equal slices.
At least 3 radius cuts are needed to divide into 3 equal slices.

title: Minimum Operations to Make the Array Increasing
description:
You are given an integer array `nums` (0-indexed). In one operation, you can choose an element of the array and increment it by 1.

An array `nums` is strictly increasing if `nums[i] < nums[i+1]` for all `0 <= i < nums.length - 1`.

Return the minimum number of operations needed to make `nums` strictly increasing.
hints: Iterate from left to right. Whenever nums[i] <= nums[i-1], greedily bump nums[i] to nums[i-1] + 1.

test_cases.explanation: Increment nums[1] to 2 (1 op), nums[2] to 3 (2 ops). Total operations = 3.
nums[2] becomes 6 (4 ops), nums[3] becomes 7 (3 ops), nums[4] becomes 8 (7 ops). Total = 14 ops.

title: Find Closest Number to Zero
description: Given an integer array `nums` of size `n`, return the number with the value closest to `0` in `nums`. If there are multiple answers, return the number with the largest value.
hints: Track the minimum absolute distance, and break ties by choosing the maximum value.

test_cases.explanation: The distance from 1 to 0 is 1, which is the closest.
Both 1 and -1 are at distance 1 from 0. 1 has the larger value, so it is returned.

title: Intersection of Multiple Arrays
description: Given a 2D integer array `nums` where `nums[i]` is a non-empty array of distinct positive integers, return the list of integers that are present in each array of `nums` sorted in ascending order.
constraints: All the values of nums[i] are unique.
hints: Find the set intersection of all rows, then sort the result.

test_cases.explanation: The integers 3 and 4 are present in each array: [3, 4].
There are no integers present in both arrays, so return [].

title: Rearrange Characters to Make Target String
description:
You are given two 0-indexed strings `s` and `target`. You can take some letters from `s` and rearrange them to form new strings.

Return the maximum number of copies of `target` that can be formed by taking letters from `s` and rearranging them.
constraints: s and target consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Count character frequencies in s and target. The answer is min(s_count[c] // target_count[c]) across all characters in target.

test_cases.explanation: We can form 2 copies of 'code' using the letters available.
We can form 1 copy of 'abc'.

title: Calculate Amount Paid in Taxes
description:
You are given a 0-indexed 2D integer array `brackets` where `brackets[i] = [upper_i, percent_i]` means the `i`-th tax bracket has an upper bound of `upper_i` and is taxed at a rate of `percent_i%`. The brackets are sorted by upper bound (`upper_{i-1} < upper_i`).

Tax is assessed progressively: the first bracket taxes income up to `upper_0`, the second taxes income between `upper_0` and `upper_1`, and so on. No tax is charged on income above `income`.

Return the total tax paid. Answers within `10^-5` of the actual answer are accepted.
hints: Iterate through brackets and calculate the taxable portion in each bracket: min(income, upper) - prev_upper.

test_cases.explanation: First 3 dollars taxed at 50% ($1.50). Next 4 dollars (3 to 7) taxed at 10% ($0.40). Remaining 3 dollars (7 to 10) taxed at 25% ($0.75). Total tax = $2.65.
First 1 dollar taxed at 0% ($0). Next 1 dollar taxed at 25% ($0.25). Total tax = $0.25.

title: Greatest English Letter in Upper and Lower Case
description:
Given a string of English letters `s`, return the greatest English letter which occurs as both a lowercase and uppercase letter in `s`. The returned letter should be in uppercase. If no such letter exists, return an empty string `""`.

An English letter `b` is greater than another letter `a` if `b` appears after `a` in the English alphabet.
constraints: s consists of lowercase and uppercase English letters.
hints: Check from 'Z' down to 'A' whether both the lowercase and uppercase forms are present in s.

test_cases.explanation: The letter 'E' is the only letter to appear in both lower and upper case.
'R' appears in both lower and upper case, as does 'A'. 'R' is greater than 'A'.

title: Make Array Zero by Subtracting Equal Amounts
description:
You are given a non-negative integer array `nums`. In one operation, you must:
1. Choose a positive integer `x` such that `x` is less than or equal to the smallest non-zero element in `nums`.
2. Subtract `x` from every positive element in `nums`.

Return the minimum number of operations to make every element in `nums` equal to `0`.
hints: Each operation can eliminate exactly one distinct positive value from the array. The answer is simply the number of distinct positive values.

test_cases.explanation: The distinct non-zero elements are 1, 3, and 5. In 3 operations, all elements can be reduced to 0.
Each element in nums is already 0 so no operations are needed.

title: Merge Similar Items
description:
You are given two 2D integer arrays, `items1` and `items2`, representing two sets of items. Each array `items[i] = [value_i, weight_i]` denotes that the item with value `value_i` has weight `weight_i`. The values of all items in each array are unique.

Return a 2D integer array `ret` where `ret[i] = [value_i, weight_i]`, with `weight_i` being the sum of weights of all items with value `value_i`. `ret` should be returned in ascending order by value.
constraints: All values in items1 are unique, and all values in items2 are unique.
hints: Use a hash map to aggregate weights for each value, then sort by value.

test_cases.explanation: Item with value 1 has weight 1 + 5 = 6. Value 3 has weight 8 + 1 = 9. Value 4 has weight 5. Output: [[1, 6], [3, 9], [4, 5]].

title: Remove Letter To Equalize Frequency
description:
You are given a 0-indexed string `word`, consisting of lowercase English letters. You need to select one index and remove the letter at that index from `word` so that the frequency of every letter present in `word` is equal.

Return `true` if it is possible to remove one letter so that the frequency of all letters in `word` are equal, and `false` otherwise.

Note that the frequency of a letter `x` is the number of times it occurs in the string, and you must remove exactly one letter.
constraints: word consists of lowercase English letters only.
hints: Since the string is small, try removing each character one by one and check if all remaining frequencies are equal.

test_cases.explanation: Remove one 'c' to get 'abc' where each letter has frequency 1.
Removing any letter leaves one letter with frequency 1 and the other with frequency 2, which are unequal.

title: Number of Common Factors
description:
Given two positive integers `a` and `b`, return the number of common factors of `a` and `b`.

An integer `x` is a common factor of `a` and `b` if `x` divides both `a` and `b`.
hints: Iterate through 1 to min(a, b) and count how many values divide both a and b.

test_cases.explanation: The common factors of 12 and 6 are 1, 2, 3, 6 (4 common factors).
The common factors of 25 and 30 are 1, 5 (2 common factors).

title: Circular Sentence
description:
A sentence is a list of words that are separated by a single space with no leading or trailing spaces.

A sentence is circular if:
- The last character of each word is equal to the first character of the next word.
- The last character of the last word is equal to the first character of the first word.

Given a string `sentence`, return `true` if it is circular, or `false` otherwise.
constraints: sentence consists of only lowercase English letters and spaces.
The words in sentence are separated by a single space.
hints: Split into words, and verify word[i][-1] == word[(i+1)%n][0] for all i.

test_cases.explanation: The words are [leetcode, exercises, sound, delightful]. 'e' == 'e', 's' == 's', 'd' == 'd', and 'l' == 'l' (last word connects to first word).
The last character 'e' matches the first character 'e', so it is circular.

title: Number of Unequal Triplets in Array
description:
You are given a 0-indexed array of positive integers `nums`. Find the number of triplets `(i, j, k)` such that `0 <= i < j < k < nums.length`, and:
- `nums[i] != nums[j]`
- `nums[i] != nums[k]`
- `nums[j] != nums[k]`

Return the number of such triplets.
hints: Group identical numbers. For each distinct group, the number of triplets formed is (elements before) * (count in group) * (elements after).

test_cases.explanation: Triplets with distinct values: (0, 2, 4), (1, 2, 4), (2, 3, 4). Output = 3.
No unequal triplets can be formed, so return 0.

title: Difference Between Element Sum and Digit Sum of an Array
description:
You are given a positive integer array `nums`.
- The element sum is the sum of all elements in `nums`.
- The digit sum is the sum of all the digits (not necessarily distinct) that appear in `nums`.

Return the absolute difference between the element sum and digit sum of `nums`.
hints: Compute sum(nums) and sum(int(d) for x in nums for d in str(x)), then return the absolute difference.

test_cases.explanation: Element sum is 10, digit sum is 10. |10 - 10| = 0.

title: Take Gifts From the Richest Pile
description:
You are given an integer array `gifts` denoting the number of gifts in various piles. Every second, you do the following:
- Choose the pile with the maximum number of gifts.
- If there is more than one pile with the maximum number of gifts, choose any.
- Leave behind the floor of the square root of the number of gifts in the pile. Take the rest of the gifts.

Return the number of gifts remaining after `k` seconds.
hints: Use a max heap or repeatedly find the maximum element and replace it with floor(sqrt(max)).

test_cases.explanation: In 4 steps, max values reduced: 100 -> 10, 64 -> 8, 25 -> 5, 10 -> 3. Sum of remaining gifts is 5 + 8 + 9 + 4 + 3 = 29.
Square root of 1 is 1, so all piles remain 1. Sum is 4.

title: Row With Maximum Ones
description:
Given a `m x n` binary matrix `mat`, find the 0-indexed position of the row that contains the maximum count of ones, and the number of ones in that row.

In the case that there are multiple rows that have the maximum count of ones, the row with the smallest row number should be selected.

Return an array containing the index of the row, and the number of ones in it.
hints: Count ones in each row and track the best (count, -row_idx).

test_cases.explanation: Both rows have 1 one. The smallest row index is 0, so return [0, 1].
Row 1 has the maximum number of ones (2). Output is [1, 2].

title: Find the Width of Columns of a Grid
description:
You are given a 0-indexed `m x n` integer matrix `grid`. The width of a column is the maximum length of its integers when converted to a string.

For example, if `grid = [[-10], [3], [12]]`, the only column has width 3 because `-10` has length 3.

Return an integer array `ans` of size `n` where `ans[c]` is the width of the `c`-th column.
hints: For each column c, compute max(len(str(grid[r][c])) for r in range(m)).

test_cases.explanation: Column 0 has values 1 (len 1), 22 (len 2), 333 (len 3). Max width is 3.
Column 0 has max len 3 ('-15'), column 1 has max len 1 ('1'), column 2 has max len 2 ('12', '-2'). Output is [3, 1, 2].

title: Find the Distinct Difference Array
description:
You are given a 0-indexed array `nums` of length `n`.

The distinct difference array of `nums` is an array `diff` of length `n` such that `diff[i]` is the number of distinct elements in the prefix `nums[0...i]` minus the number of distinct elements in the suffix `nums[i + 1...n - 1]`.

Return the distinct difference array of `nums`.

Note that `nums[i + 1...n - 1]` is empty for `i = n - 1`, and an empty suffix contains 0 distinct elements.
hints: Use sets to count distinct elements in nums[:i+1] and nums[i+1:].

title: Determine the Winner of a Bowling Game
description:
You are given two 0-indexed integer arrays `player1` and `player2`, that represent the number of pins that player 1 and player 2 hit in a bowling game, which consists of `n` turns.

The score of each player in a turn `i` is:
- `2 * player[i]` if the player hit 10 pins in turn `i - 1` or `i - 2`.
- `player[i]` otherwise.

The overall score is the sum of the scores across all `n` turns.

Return:
- `1` if the score of player 1 is strictly greater than player 2.
- `2` if player 2 is strictly greater than player 1.
- `0` in case of a draw.
hints: Simulate each player's score tracking whether the preceding two rounds included a 10.

test_cases.explanation: Player 1 score: 4 + 10 + 2*7 + 2*9 = 46. Player 2 score: 6 + 5 + 2 + 3 = 16. Player 1 wins (return 1).
Player 1 score = 21. Player 2 score = 8 + 10 + 2*10 + 2*2 = 42. Player 2 wins (return 2).

title: Maximum Sum With Exactly K Elements
description:
You are given a 0-indexed integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. Your task is to perform the following operation exactly `k` times in order to maximize your score:
1. Select an element `m` from `nums`.
2. Remove the selected element `m` from the array.
3. Add a new element with a value of `m + 1` to the array.
4. Increase your score by `m`.

Return the maximum score you can achieve after applying the operation exactly `k` times.
hints: Always greedily choose the maximum element m in nums. The score will be m + (m+1) + ... + (m+k-1) = k*m + k*(k-1)//2.

test_cases.explanation: Choose 5, score = 5, nums has 6. Choose 6, score = 5 + 6 = 11, nums has 7. Choose 7, score = 11 + 7 = 18.
Choose 5, score += 5. Choose 6, score += 6. Total score = 11.

title: Find the Maximum Divisibility Score
description:
You are given two 0-indexed integer arrays `nums` and `divisors`.

The divisibility score of `divisors[i]` is the number of indices `j` such that `nums[j]` is divisible by `divisors[i]`.

Return the integer `divisors[i]` with the maximum divisibility score. If there is more than one integer with the maximum score, return the minimum of them.
hints: For each divisor d, count how many elements in nums have nums[j] % d == 0. Pick the one with highest score, tie-breaking by smaller d.

test_cases.explanation: 5 divides none (0). 2 divides 4 (1). 3 divides 9, 3, 9 (3). Max score is 3 with divisor 3.
5 divides 20, 10 (2). 7 divides 14, 21 (2). Both have score 2; the smaller divisor is 5.

title: Semi-Ordered Permutation
description:
You are given a 0-indexed permutation of `n` integers `nums`.

A permutation is called semi-ordered if the first number equals `1` and the last number equals `n`. You can perform adjacent swaps.

Return the minimum number of operations to make `nums` a semi-ordered permutation.
hints: Find index of 1 (pos1) and index of n (posN).
If pos1 < posN, swaps needed = pos1 + (n - 1 - posN).
If pos1 > posN, they cross each other, saving 1 swap: pos1 + (n - 1 - posN) - 1.

test_cases.explanation: Swap 2 and 1 -> [1, 2, 4, 3], swap 4 and 3 -> [1, 2, 3, 4]. Total swaps = 2.
Swapping 1 to position 0 and 4 to position 3 takes 3 operations.

title: Minimize String Length
description:
Given a 0-indexed string `s`, repeatedly perform the following operation any number of times:
1. Choose an index `i` in the string.
2. Delete the closest occurrence of character `s[i]` to its left (if any).
3. Delete the closest occurrence of character `s[i]` to its right (if any).

Return the minimum length of the string after minimizing it.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters.
hints: Notice that duplicate characters can always be eliminated until only one copy of each distinct character remains. The answer is the number of distinct characters in s.

test_cases.explanation: Operation on 'a' deletes duplicate 'a's, leaving 'abc' of length 3.
Deleting the duplicate 'b' leaves 'cbd' of length 3.

title: Minimum Size Subarray in Infinite Array
description:
You are given a 0-indexed array `nums` and an integer `target`. An infinite array is formed by repeating `nums` infinitely to the right.

Return the minimum length of a subarray in the infinite array whose sum equals `target`. If no such subarray exists, return `-1`.
hints: Let total = sum(nums). Any subarray sum can be broken into k * total + remainder, where remainder is the sum of a subarray spanning at most 2 * n elements.

test_cases.explanation: The subarray [2, 3] has sum 5 and length 2.
The subarray [1, 1, 2] or [1, 3] (wrapping from end to start) has sum 4 and length 2.

title: Count Complete Subarrays in an Array
description:
You are given an array `nums` consisting of positive integers.

We call a subarray of an array complete if the following condition is satisfied:
- The number of distinct elements in the subarray is equal to the number of distinct elements in the whole array.

Return the number of complete subarrays.
hints: Calculate total distinct elements k. Use a sliding window: once a window nums[left..right] contains k distinct elements, every window extending to the end (nums[left..end]) is also complete.

test_cases.explanation: Total distinct elements is 3 ({1, 2, 3}). The complete subarrays are [1, 3, 1, 2], [1, 3, 1, 2, 2], [3, 1, 2], and [3, 1, 2, 2]. Total = 4.
Total distinct elements is 1. Every subarray is complete (10 complete subarrays).

title: Number of Pairs of Interchangeable Rectangles
description:
You are given `n` rectangles represented by a 0-indexed 2D integer array `rectangles`, where `rectangles[i] = [width_i, height_i]` denotes the width and height of the `i`-th rectangle.

Two rectangles `i` and `j` (`i < j`) are considered interchangeable if they have the same width-to-height ratio: `width_i / height_i == width_j / height_j`.

Return the number of pairs of interchangeable rectangles.
hints: Reduce each ratio w / h to simplest form by dividing by gcd(w, h), and count frequencies in a hash map.

test_cases.explanation: All 4 rectangles have ratio 1/2. Number of pairs = 4 * 3 // 2 = 6.
No two rectangles share the same ratio. Return 0.

title: Difference Between Ones and Zeros in Row and Column
description:
You are given a 0-indexed `m x n` binary matrix `grid`.

A 0-indexed `m x n` difference matrix `diff` is created with the same dimension where:
- `diff[i][j] = onesRow_i + onesCol_j - zerosRow_i - zerosCol_j`

Return the difference matrix `diff`.
hints: Notice zerosRow_i = n - onesRow_i and zerosCol_j = m - onesCol_j. Thus diff[i][j] = 2 * onesRow_i + 2 * onesCol_j - n - m.

test_cases.explanation: All elements are 1. diff[i][j] = 2 * 3 + 2 * 2 - 3 - 2 = 5 for all cells.

title: Determine if a Cell Is Reachable at a Given Time
description:
You are given four integers `sx`, `sy`, `fx`, `fy`, and a non-negative integer `t`.

In an infinite 2D grid, you start at the cell `(sx, sy)`. Each second, you must move to any of its 8 adjacent cells (horizontal, vertical, or diagonal).

Return `true` if you can reach the cell `(fx, fy)` after exactly `t` seconds, or `false` otherwise.
hints: The minimum time to reach (fx, fy) with Chebyshev distance is max(abs(sx - fx), abs(sy - fy)).
Be careful with the special case where start equals finish: if sx == fx and sy == fy and t == 1, it is impossible because you must move to an adjacent cell and cannot return in 1 step.

test_cases.explanation: Min distance is max(|2-7|, |4-7|) = max(5, 3) = 5. Since t = 6 >= 5, it is reachable.
Min distance is max(4, 2) = 4. Since t = 3 < 4, it is not reachable.

title: Solving Questions With Brainpower
description:
You are given a 0-indexed 2D integer array `questions` where `questions[i] = [points_i, brainpower_i]`.

You are solving questions in order. If you solve question `i`, you gain `points_i` points, but you will be unable to solve each of the next `brainpower_i` questions. If you skip question `i`, you get 0 points and may solve the next question.

Return the maximum points you can earn.
hints: Work backwards from the last question to the first: dp[i] = max(dp[i+1], points[i] + dp[i + brainpower[i] + 1]).

test_cases.explanation: Solve Q0 (+3 pts, skip Q1 and Q2), then solve Q3 (+2 pts). Total = 5 pts.
Solve Q0 (+1, skip Q1), solve Q2 (+3, skip Q3), solve Q4 (+5). Total = 1 + 3 + 5 = 9.

title: Destroying Asteroids
description:
You are given an integer `mass`, which represents the initial mass of a planet. You are also given an integer array `asteroids`, where `asteroids[i]` is the mass of the `i`-th asteroid.

You can collide the planet with the asteroids in any arbitrary order. If the mass of the planet is greater than or equal to the mass of the asteroid, the asteroid is destroyed and the planet gains the mass of the asteroid. Otherwise, the planet is destroyed.

Return `true` if all asteroids can be destroyed, or `false` otherwise.
hints: Greedily sort asteroids in ascending order and collide with smallest ones first to maximize growth.

test_cases.explanation: Planet mass reaches 5 + 4 + 4 = 13, then asteroid 23 destroys planet. Return false.

title: Maximum Bags With Full Capacity of Rocks
description:
You have `n` bags numbered from `0` to `n - 1`. You are given two 0-indexed integer arrays `capacity` and `rocks`. The `i`-th bag can hold a maximum of `capacity[i]` rocks and currently contains `rocks[i]` rocks. You are also given an integer `additionalRocks`, the number of additional rocks you can place in any of the bags.

Return the maximum number of bags that could have full capacity after placing the additional rocks in some bags.
hints: Calculate needed rocks capacity[i] - rocks[i] for each bag. Sort needed rocks ascending and greedily fill the smallest deficits first.

test_cases.explanation: Needed: [1, 1, 0, 1]. Bag 2 is already full. Add 1 rock to bag 0, 1 rock to bag 1. Now 3 bags are full.
All 3 bags can easily be filled.

title: Longest Ideal Subsequence
description:
You are given a string `s` consisting of lowercase letters and an integer `k`. We call a string `t` ideal if `t` is a subsequence of the string `s` and the absolute difference in the alphabet order of every two adjacent letters in `t` is less than or equal to `k`.

Return the length of the longest ideal subsequence.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Maintain an array dp of size 26 where dp[c] is the length of the longest ideal subsequence ending with character c.

test_cases.explanation: The longest ideal subsequence is 'abcd' (length 4), since adjacent character differences are <= 2.
The whole string 'abcd' is ideal of length 4.

title: Count Number of Distinct Integers After Reverse Operations
description:
You are given an array `nums` consisting of positive integers.

You take each integer in the array, reverse its digits, and add the reversed number to the end of the array. You should apply this operation to every integer originally in `nums`.

Return the number of distinct integers in the final array.
hints: Put all nums[i] and int(str(nums[i])[::-1]) into a set, and return the size of the set.

test_cases.explanation: Originals: [1, 13, 10, 12, 31]. Reversed: [1, 31, 1, 21, 13]. Distinct values: {1, 10, 12, 13, 21, 31} -> 6 distinct integers.
Only the distinct integer 2 is present (reversed 2 is 2). Output = 1.

title: Minimize Maximum of Array
description:
You are given a 0-indexed integer array `nums` of length `n`.

In one operation, you can choose an integer `i` such that `1 <= i < n` and `nums[i] > 0`, decrease `nums[i]` by 1, and increase `nums[i - 1]` by 1.

Return the minimum possible value of the maximum integer of `nums` after any number of operations.
hints: Operations only shift values from right to left. The prefix sum sum(nums[:i+1]) cannot decrease, so the average ceil(prefix_sum / (i + 1)) is a lower bound for each prefix.

test_cases.explanation: Can balance to max value 5 (e.g. [5, 5, 2, 5]). Return 5.
Cannot decrease nums[0]. Maximum value remains 10.

title: Bitwise XOR of All Pairings
description:
You are given two 0-indexed arrays, `nums1` and `nums2`, consisting of non-negative integers. There exists another array, `nums3`, which contains the bitwise XOR of all pairings of integers between `nums1` and `nums2` (every integer in `nums1` is paired with every integer in `nums2` exactly once).

Return the bitwise XOR of all integers in `nums3`.
hints: Each element in nums1 appears len(nums2) times, and each element in nums2 appears len(nums1) times. If length is odd, XOR all elements; if even, they cancel out to 0.

test_cases.explanation: len(nums2) is even (4), so nums1 elements cancel out. len(nums1) is odd (3), so nums2 elements XOR together: 10 ^ 2 ^ 5 ^ 0 = 13.
Both lengths are even, so all elements cancel out to 0.

title: Number of Subarrays That Match a Pattern I
description:
You are given a 0-indexed integer array `nums` of size `n`, and a 0-indexed integer array `pattern` of size `m` consisting of integers `-1`, `0`, and `1`.

A subarray `nums[i..i + m]` of size `m + 1` matches `pattern` if for all `k` from `0` to `m - 1`:
- `nums[i + k + 1] > nums[i + k]` if `pattern[k] == 1`
- `nums[i + k + 1] == nums[i + k]` if `pattern[k] == 0`
- `nums[i + k + 1] < nums[i + k]` if `pattern[k] == -1`

Return the count of subarrays that match the pattern.
hints: Transform nums into an array of transitions diff[k] = 1 if nums[k+1] > nums[k] else (-1 if nums[k+1] < nums[k] else 0), then count matching windows.

test_cases.explanation: Subarrays of size 3 that increase twice: [1,2,3], [2,3,4], [3,4,5], [4,5,6] (4 subarrays).
Matches at [1, 4, 4, 1] and [3, 5, 5, 3] (2 subarrays).

title: Minimum Penalty for a Shop
description:
You are given the customer visit log of a shop represented by a 0-indexed string `customers` consisting only of characters `'N'` and `'Y'`:
- if the `i`-th character is `'Y'`, it means that customers came at the `i`-th hour
- if the `i`-th character is `'N'`, it means no customers came at the `i`-th hour

If the shop closes at the `j`-th hour (`0 <= j <= n`):
- For every hour when the shop was open and no customers came, the penalty increases by 1.
- For every hour when the shop was closed and customers came, the penalty increases by 1.

Return the earliest hour at which the shop must be closed to incur a minimum penalty.
constraints: customers consists only of characters 'Y' and 'N'.
hints: Precompute suffix counts of 'Y' and prefix counts of 'N' to evaluate the penalty at each hour j in O(1) time.

test_cases.explanation: Closing at hour 2 gives penalty 1 (from hour 2 closed with 'Y' at hour 3, plus 'N' at hour 2). Minimum penalty is 1 at hour 2.
Closing at hour 0 gives penalty 0 because no customers came. Best hour is 0.

title: Minimum Number of Swaps to Make the Binary String Balanced
description:
You are given a 0-indexed string `s` of even length `n`. The string consists of exactly `n / 2` opening brackets `'['` and `n / 2` closing brackets `']'`.

A string is called balanced if and only if it is a regular bracket sequence.

Return the minimum number of swaps to make `s` balanced. You can swap the brackets at any two indices.
constraints: The number of '[' in s equals the number of ']'.
hints: Count unmatched closing brackets. Each swap can fix two pairs of mismatched brackets, so (max_imbalance + 1) // 2.

test_cases.explanation: Swap index 0 and 3: '[]][', then balanced.
Two swaps are needed to fix 3 unmatched brackets: (3 + 1) // 2 = 2.

title: Find All Groups of Farmland
description:
You are given a 0-indexed `m x n` binary matrix `land` where a `0` represents a forest area and a `1` represents a farmland area.

Farmland occurs in rectangular groups of connected 1s that do not touch other farmlands vertically or horizontally.

Return a 2D array containing the 4-index coordinates `[r1, c1, r2, c2]` of each farmland group (top-left and bottom-right corners), in any order.
hints: A cell (r, c) is the top-left of a farmland group if land[r][c] == 1 and it has no 1 above or to its left.

test_cases.explanation: Two farmland groups: top-left [0, 0, 0, 0] and bottom-right [1, 1, 2, 2].
One single farmland group from [0, 0] to [1, 1].

title: Watering Plants
description:
You want to water `n` plants in your garden with a watering can. The plants are arranged in a row from `0` to `n - 1`. A river is located at `x = -1`.

You start at the river with a fully filled watering can of capacity `capacity`. Watering plant `i` takes `plants[i]` units of water. If you do not have enough water to completely water plant `i`, you must walk back to the river to refill and return to plant `i`.

Return the total number of steps to water all the plants.
hints: Simulate the walk: step forward 1 each plant. When remaining water < plants[i], add 2 * i steps for the round trip back to the river.

test_cases.explanation: Steps taken: 1, 2, refill at river (2*2 = 4 extra steps), 3, 4 -> Total = 14 steps.
Total steps = 30.

title: Watering Plants II
description:
Alice and Bob want to water `n` plants in a row. Alice starts at plant `0` (walking right) with capacity `capacityA`, and Bob starts at plant `n - 1` (walking left) with capacity `capacityB`. They move simultaneously.

If one does not have enough water to completely water their current plant, they refill to full (costing 1 refill). If they meet at the same plant, whoever has more water waters it; if tied, Alice waters it.

Return the number of times Alice or Bob must refill their watering can.
hints: Use two pointers l = 0 and r = n - 1 moving towards the middle.

test_cases.explanation: Alice waters plants 0 and 1 without refilling. Bob waters plants 3 and 2 without refilling. 0 refills needed.
Alice refills once, Bob refills once. Total refills = 2.

title: Execution of All Suffix Instructions Staying in a Grid
description:
There is an `n x n` grid, with the top-left cell at `(0, 0)` and bottom-right at `(n - 1, n - 1)`. You are given the integer `n` and an integer array `startPos` where `startPos = [start_row, start_col]`.

You are also given a string `s` of length `m`, consisting of 'L', 'R', 'U', 'D'.

Return an array `ans` of size `m` where `ans[i]` is the number of instructions you can execute starting from instruction `i` until you either move off the grid or execute all remaining instructions in `s`.
hints: For each starting index i, simulate the robot step by step until it goes out of bounds or s ends.

test_cases.explanation: From index 0: R moves to (0, 2), next R moves off grid (1 step). Output is [1, 5, 4, 3, 1, 0].
Output is [4, 1, 0, 0].

title: Intervals Between Identical Elements
description:
You are given a 0-indexed integer array `arr` of size `n`.

The interval between two elements is the absolute difference between their indices. For each index `i`, find the sum of intervals between `i` and all other indices `j` such that `arr[i] == arr[j]` (`i != j`).

Return an array `ans` of length `n` where `ans[i]` is this sum of intervals.
hints: Group indices by their value. For each value, prefix sums of indices allow computing sum of distances in O(1) per index.

test_cases.explanation: For index 0 (val 2), index 4 also has 2. Interval = |0 - 4| = 4. ans = [4, 2, 7, 2, 4, 4, 5].

title: Minimum Operations to Make Array Equal II
description:
You are given two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2` of equal length `n` and an integer `k`. You can choose two distinct indices `i` and `j` and increment `nums1[i]` by `k` while decrementing `nums1[j]` by `k`.

Return the minimum number of operations to make `nums1` equal to `nums2`, or `-1` if it is impossible.
hints: If k == 0, check if nums1 == nums2. Otherwise, check that (nums1[i] - nums2[i]) % k == 0 for all i, and total positive differences equal total negative differences.

test_cases.explanation: Diffs are +3, 0, -6, +3. Sum of positive diffs / k is (3 + 3) / 3 = 2 ops.
Sum of nums1 is 18, sum of nums2 is 13. Impossible, return -1.

title: Find the Substring With Maximum Cost
description:
You are given a string `s`, a string `chars` of distinct characters, and an integer array `vals` of the same length as `chars`.

The cost of a substring is the sum of the values of each character in the substring. Characters present in `chars` have the corresponding value in `vals`, and any other English letter has value equal to its 1-based alphabet position (`'a' -> 1, 'b' -> 2, ..., 'z' -> 26`).

Return the maximum cost among all substrings of `s`. The cost of an empty substring is `0`.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
chars consists of distinct lowercase English letters.
hints: Map each character in s to its integer value, then apply Kadane's algorithm to find maximum subarray sum (bounded below by 0).

test_cases.explanation: 'a' has value 1, 'd' has value -1010. Best substring is 'aa' with cost 1 + 1 = 2.
All characters have negative cost. The empty substring has cost 0.

title: Mice and Cheese
description:
There are two mice and `n` different types of cheese, each type with a piece. You are given two 0-indexed integer arrays `reward1` and `reward2` where `reward1[i]` and `reward2[i]` represent the points the first and second mouse receive if they eat the `i`-th cheese respectively. You are also given a non-negative integer `k`.

The first mouse must eat exactly `k` pieces of cheese, and the second mouse eats the remaining `n - k` pieces.

Return the maximum total points the mice can receive.
hints: Initially assume mouse 2 eats all cheese (sum(reward2)). Giving cheese i to mouse 1 gains reward1[i] - reward2[i]. Greedily pick the top k largest gains.

test_cases.explanation: Mouse 1 eats cheese 2 and 3 (+3, +4). Mouse 2 eats cheese 0 and 1 (+4, +4). Total = 15.
Mouse 2 eats all cheese: 1 + 2 = 3.

title: Count the Number of Beautiful Subarrays
description:
You are given a 0-indexed integer array `nums`. A subarray of `nums` is called beautiful if you can make all its elements equal to 0 by repeatedly subtracting the same power of two from two different elements in the subarray.

An array can be reduced to 0 this way if and only if every bit position has an even number of set bits (i.e. the bitwise XOR sum of the subarray is 0).

Return the number of beautiful subarrays in `nums`.
hints: The condition is equivalent to XOR sum of the subarray being 0. Track running prefix XOR counts with a hash map.

test_cases.explanation: Subarrays with XOR sum 0: [4, 3, 1, 2], [3, 1, 2], [4] with nothing, etc. Total = 4.
No non-empty subarray has XOR sum 0. Return 0.

title: Find the Prefix Common Array of Two Arrays
description:
You are given two 0-indexed integer permutations `A` and `B` of length `n`.

A prefix common array of `A` and `B` is an array `C` such that `C[i]` is equal to the count of numbers that are present at or before the index `i` in both `A` and `B`.

Return the prefix common array of `A` and `B`.
constraints: A and B are permutations of integers from 1 to n.
hints: Maintain a frequency set of elements seen in both arrays up to index i. When an element is seen twice, increment the common counter.

test_cases.explanation: At i=0: A[0]=1, B[0]=3 (common 0). At i=1: 1 and 3 are in both (common 2). At i=2: 1, 2, 3 in both (3). At i=3: all 4 in both (4). Output: [0, 2, 3, 4].
Prefix common array is [0, 1, 3].

title: Minimum Processing Time
description:
You have `n` processors, each having 4 cores. You are given a 0-indexed integer array `processorTime` representing the time each processor becomes available, and a 0-indexed integer array `tasks` of length `4 * n` representing the execution time of each task.

Each core of each processor can execute at most one task. All cores within a processor start at `processorTime[i]`. The processor finishes all its 4 tasks when the longest task assigned to it finishes (`processorTime[i] + max(task_times)`).

Return the minimum time when all processors finish their assigned tasks.
hints: Pair the processors available earliest with the longest tasks to balance completion times.

test_cases.explanation: Processor 0 (time 8) gets largest tasks [8, 7, 5, 4] -> finish at 8 + 8 = 16. Processor 1 (time 10) gets [3, 2, 2, 1] -> finish at 10 + 3 = 13. Max is 16.
Processor 10 gets [8, 5, 4, 3] -> 10 + 8 = 18. Processor 20 gets [3, 2, 2, 1] -> 20 + 3 = 23. Max is 23.

title: Minimum Array Length After Pair Removals
description:
Given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, you can repeatedly select two indices `i` and `j` such that `i < j` and `nums[i] < nums[j]`, and remove both elements.

Return the minimum length of `nums` after any number of operations.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order.
hints: The maximum frequency of any element determines the result: if max_freq <= n // 2, all elements can be paired up (leaving n % 2 elements). Otherwise, 2 * max_freq - n elements must remain.

test_cases.explanation: Remove 1 and 3, then 4 and 9. Array length becomes 0.
Pair (2, 6) and (3, 9). Final length is 0.

title: Find Polygon With the Largest Perimeter
description:
You are given an array of positive integers `nums` of length `n`. A polygon is a closed plane figure consisting of at least 3 sides. The longest side of a polygon is strictly less than the sum of all other sides.

Return the largest possible perimeter of a polygon whose side lengths can be formed from `nums`, or `-1` if it is not possible to form a polygon.
hints: Sort the array. Check from the largest element downwards whether the sum of all smaller elements exceeds it.

test_cases.explanation: All 3 sides equal 5, polygon exists: perimeter = 15.
Sort: [1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 12, 50]. The largest valid polygon has sides [1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 12] with sum 24 > 12 -> perimeter = 12 + 12 = 24.

title: Divide Array Into Arrays With Max Difference
description:
You are given an integer array `nums` of size `n` where `n` is a multiple of 3 and a positive integer `k`.

Divide the array into `n / 3` arrays of size 3 such that the difference between any two elements in each array is less than or equal to `k`.

Return a 2D array containing all the arrays. If it is impossible, return an empty array `[]`.
hints: Sort nums. If any triplet nums[i..i+2] has nums[i+2] - nums[i] > k, then no valid partition exists.

test_cases.explanation: Sorted: [1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 7]. Triplet [3, 3, 7] has diff 7 - 3 = 4 > 3. Impossible -> [].

title: Sequential Digits
description:
An integer has sequential digits if and only if each digit in the number is one more than the previous digit.

Return a sorted list of all the integers in the range `[low, high]` inclusive that have sequential digits.
hints: Generate all sequential numbers by sliding windows over '123456789' for lengths 1 through 9, then filter those in [low, high].

test_cases.explanation: Sequential numbers in [100, 300] are 123 and 234.

title: Special Array II
description:
An array is considered special if every pair of its adjacent elements contains two numbers with different parity (one even and one odd).

You are given an array of integers `nums` and a 2D integer matrix `queries` where `queries[i] = [from_i, to_i]`. For each query `i`, determine if the subarray `nums[from_i..to_i]` is special.

Return an array of booleans `answer` where `answer[i]` is `true` if `nums[from_i..to_i]` is special, and `false` otherwise.
hints: Compute a prefix sum of bad adjacent pairs where nums[i] % 2 == nums[i+1] % 2. A query [from, to] is special if bad[to] - bad[from] == 0.

test_cases.explanation: Subarray [3, 4, 1, 2, 6] has adjacent elements 2 and 6 with the same parity (both even), so query is false.
[0, 2]: [4, 3, 1] has adjacent (3, 1) both odd -> false. [2, 3]: [1, 6] has alternating parity -> true. Output: [false, true].

title: Find the Number of Good Pairs II
description:
You are given 2 integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2` of lengths `n` and `m` respectively, and a positive integer `k`.

A pair `(i, j)` is called good if `nums1[i]` is divisible by `nums2[j] * k` (`0 <= i <= n - 1`, `0 <= j <= m - 1`).

Return the total number of good pairs.
hints: Count frequencies of nums2[j] * k. For each number x in nums1, iterate through all of its divisors in O(sqrt(x)) time.

test_cases.explanation: Only (3, 0) is good (12 is divisible by 2 * 3 = 6). Total = 2 good pairs.

title: Average Waiting Time
description:
There is a restaurant with a single chef. You are given an array `customers`, where `customers[i] = [arrival_i, time_i]`:
- `arrival_i` is the arrival time of the `i`-th customer.
- `time_i` is the time needed to prepare the order of the `i`-th customer.

Customers are served in arrival order. Return the average waiting time of all customers. Answers within `10^-5` of the actual answer are accepted.
hints: Track chef finish time. The wait for each customer is finish_time - arrival_time.

test_cases.explanation: Customer 1 waits 2 (finished at 3). Customer 2 waits 6 (finished at 8). Customer 3 waits 7 (finished at 11). Average = (2 + 6 + 7) / 3 = 5.0.
Average waiting time = (2 + 6 + 3 + 1) / 4 = 3.25.

title: Sort the Jumbled Numbers
description:
You are given a 0-indexed integer array `mapping` of length 10 indicating the mapping of each digit from `0` to `9`. You are also given an integer array `nums`.

The mapped value of an integer is formed by replacing each digit of the integer with `mapping[digit]`.

Sort `nums` in non-decreasing order based on their mapped values. If two integers have the same mapped value, their relative order in the original array must be maintained (stable sort).
constraints: All elements of mapping are unique.
hints: Convert each number to its mapped integer value, then perform a stable sort using mapped values as keys.

test_cases.explanation: Identity mapping preserves values: [123, 456, 789].

title: Eliminate Maximum Number of Monsters
description:
You are playing a video game where you defend your city from monsters. You are given two 0-indexed integer arrays `dist` and `speed` of length `n`, where `dist[i]` and `speed[i]` are the initial distance and speed of the `i`-th monster.

You have a weapon that eliminates one monster per minute. The weapon starts fully charged and fires at minute 0, then 1, 2, etc. If a monster reaches the city at or before the minute you fire, you lose.

Return the maximum number of monsters you can eliminate before losing.
hints: Compute the arrival time for each monster: ceil(dist[i] / speed[i]). Sort times ascending and check whether time <= current_minute.

test_cases.explanation: Arrival times: [1, 3, 4]. Min 0: kill monster 0. Min 1: kill monster 1 (dist was 2 > 0). Min 2: kill monster 2. All 3 eliminated.
Arrival times: [1, 1, 2, 3]. Min 0: kill monster 0. At min 1, monster 1 arrives before weapon can fire again. Eliminated 1 monster.

title: Adding Spaces to a String
description:
You are given a 0-indexed string `s` and a 0-indexed integer array `spaces` that describes the indices in the original string where spaces will be added. Each space should be inserted before the character at the given index.

Return the modified string after the spaces have been added.
constraints: All the values of spaces are strictly increasing.
hints: Two pointers: iterate through s while tracking the current index in spaces.

test_cases.explanation: Indices 8, 13, 15 are before 'H', 'M', and 'L': 'Leetcode Helps Me Learn'.
'i code in py thon'.

test_cases.expected_output: s p a c i n g

title: Minimum Swaps to Group All 1s Together II
description:
A swap is defined as taking two distinct positions in an array and swapping the values in them.

A circular array is an array where the next element of the last element is the first element.

Given a binary circular array `nums`, return the minimum number of swaps required to group all `1`'s present in the array together at any location.
hints: Let k = sum(nums). In any window of size k in nums + nums, the number of swaps to fill the window with 1s is k - (ones in window). Find the window with maximum 1s.

test_cases.explanation: Total 1s is 3. Window [1, 1, 1] can be achieved with 1 swap (swap index 0 with 4).
Total 1s is 5. Minimum swaps is 2.

title: Range Sum of Sorted Subarray Sums
description:
You are given the array `nums` consisting of `n` positive integers. You computed the sum of all non-empty continuous subarrays from the array and then sorted them in non-decreasing order, creating a new array of `n * (n + 1) / 2` numbers.

Return the sum of the numbers from index `left` to index `right` (1-indexed) inclusive, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: Compute all subarray sums, sort them, and sum elements from index left-1 to right-1 modulo 10^9 + 7.

test_cases.explanation: Subarray sums: [1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10]. First 5 elements sum: 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 4 = 13.
Elements at index 3 and 4 are 3 and 3. Sum = 6.

title: Make String a Subsequence Using Cyclic Increments
description:
You are given two 0-indexed strings `str1` and `str2`.

In an operation, you can select a set of indices in `str1`, and for each selected index, increment the character cyclically (`'a'` becomes `'b'`, `'z'` becomes `'a'`). You can perform this operation at most once.

Return `true` if it is possible to make `str2` a subsequence of `str1`, and `false` otherwise.
constraints: str1 and str2 consist only of lowercase English letters.
hints: Two pointers: match str2[j] against str1[i]. A match occurs if str1[i] == str2[j] or (ord(str1[i]) - ord('a') + 1) % 26 == ord(str2[j]) - ord('a').

test_cases.explanation: Increment 'c' to 'd' in str1 -> 'abd'. 'ad' is a subsequence of 'abd'.
Increment 'z' -> 'a' and 'c' -> 'd' -> 'ad', which matches.

title: Move Pieces to Obtain a String
description:
You are given two strings `start` and `target`, both of length `n`. Each string consists only of the characters `'L'`, `'R'`, and `'_'`:
- The characters `'L'` and `'R'` represent pieces, where `'L'` can only move to the left if there is a blank space `'_'`, and `'R'` can only move to the right if there is a blank space `'_'`.
- The pieces cannot cross each other.

Return `true` if it is possible to obtain the string `target` by moving the pieces of the string `start` any number of times, or `false` otherwise.
constraints: start and target consist of 'L', 'R', and '_'.
hints: The sequence of non-blank characters must be identical. An 'L' in start cannot end up to the right of its target position, and an 'R' cannot end up to the left.

test_cases.explanation: Move first 'L' to index 0, move 'R's to the right. Both strings match.
'R' cannot jump over 'L', return false.

title: Magic Squares In Grid
description:
A `3 x 3` magic square is a `3 x 3` grid filled with distinct numbers from 1 to 9 such that each row, column, and both diagonals all have the same sum (15).

Given a `row x col` `grid` of integers, how many `3 x 3` contiguous magic square subgrids are there?
hints: The center of every 3x3 magic square from 1 to 9 must be 5. Check all 3x3 subgrids directly.

test_cases.explanation: The 3x3 subgrid from (0,0) to (2,2) has distinct digits 1..9 with all row/col/diag sums equal to 15. Total = 1.
Grid is smaller than 3x3, return 0.

title: Find the Student that Will Replace the Chalk
description:
There are `n` students in a class numbered `0` to `n - 1`. The teacher will give each student a problem starting with student `0`, then `1`, up to `n - 1`, and then restart from `0`.

You are given a 0-indexed integer array `chalk` and an integer `k`. There are initially `k` pieces of chalk. When student `i` solves a problem, they use `chalk[i]` pieces of chalk. If remaining chalk < `chalk[i]`, student `i` must replace the chalk.

Return the index of the student that will replace the chalk.
hints: A complete cycle uses sum(chalk) chalk. The remaining chalk is k % sum(chalk). Walk from student 0 to find who runs out.

test_cases.explanation: One full round uses 5 + 1 + 5 = 11 chalk. 22 % 11 = 0. Student 0 needs 5 pieces, but 0 is left. Student 0 replaces chalk.
One round = 10 chalk. 25 % 10 = 5. Student 0 uses 3 (2 left). Student 1 needs 4 pieces but only 2 remain. Student 1 replaces chalk.

title: Make Sum Divisible by P
description:
Given an array of positive integers `nums`, remove the smallest subarray (possibly empty) such that the sum of the remaining elements is divisible by `p`. It is not allowed to remove the whole array.

Return the length of the smallest subarray that you need to remove, or `-1` if it's impossible.
hints: Let target = sum(nums) % p. If target == 0, return 0. Otherwise, find the shortest subarray with (sum % p) == target using prefix sums and a hash map.

test_cases.explanation: Total sum = 10 (10 % 6 = 4). Removing [4] gives [3, 1, 2] with sum 6 (divisible by 6). Length = 1.
Total sum = 16 (16 % 9 = 7). Removing [5, 2] gives [6, 3] with sum 9. Length = 2.

title: Sentence Similarity III
description:
A sentence is a list of words that are separated by a single space with no leading or trailing spaces.

Two sentences `sentence1` and `sentence2` are similar if it is possible to insert an arbitrary sentence (possibly empty) inside one of these sentences such that the two sentences become equal. The inserted sentence must be separated by spaces.

Return `true` if `sentence1` and `sentence2` are similar, or `false` otherwise.
constraints: sentence1 and sentence2 consist of lowercase and uppercase English letters and spaces.
Words are separated by a single space.
hints: Compare prefix words and suffix words between the shorter sentence and the longer sentence. If matching prefix length + matching suffix length >= length of shorter sentence, return true.

test_cases.explanation: Insert 'name is' between 'My' and 'Haley' in sentence2 to get sentence1.
Cannot make them equal, return false.

title: Maximum Swap
description:
You are given an integer `num`. You can swap two digits at most once to get the maximum valued number.

Return the maximum valued number you can get.
hints: Record the last position of each digit 0-9. Scan digits from left to right; if there is a larger digit appearing later, swap with the largest one that appears latest.

test_cases.explanation: Swap 2 with 7 to get 7236.
Already maximum. Return 9973.

title: Two Best Non-Overlapping Events
description:
You are given a 0-indexed 2D integer array of `events` where `events[i] = [startTime_i, endTime_i, value_i]`. The `i`-th event starts at `startTime_i` and ends at `endTime_i`, and if you attend this event, you will receive a value of `value_i`.

You can attend at most two non-overlapping events. You can attend an event that starts at `startTime` if the previous event ended at `endTime < startTime` (strictly less).

Return the maximum sum of values that you can receive.
hints: Sort events by end time. Compute prefix maximum values. For each event, use binary search to find the latest non-overlapping previous event.

test_cases.explanation: Attend event 0 ([1, 3], val 2) and event 1 ([4, 5], val 2) for total value 4.
Attend event 2 ([1, 5], val 5) for total value 5.

title: Tuple with Same Product
description: Given an array `nums` of distinct positive integers, return the number of tuples `(a, b, c, d)` such that `a * b = c * d` where `a`, `b`, `c`, and `d` are distinct elements of `nums`, and `a != b != c != d`.
constraints: All elements in nums are distinct.
hints: Compute products for all pairs (i, j). If a product appears k times, the number of distinct 4-tuples formed is (k * (k - 1) // 2) * 8.

test_cases.explanation: 2 * 6 = 12 and 3 * 4 = 12. There are 8 valid permutations of (2, 6, 3, 4).
Products: 1*10 = 2*5 = 10 (8 tuples), 2*10 = 4*5 = 20 (8 tuples). Total = 16.

title: Find Kth Bit in Nth Binary String
description:
Given two integers `n` and `k`, binary string `S_n` is formed as follows:
- `S_1 = "0"`
- `S_i = S_{i - 1} + "1" + reverse(invert(S_{i - 1}))` for `i > 1`

Where `+` denotes concatenation, `reverse(x)` reverses `x`, and `invert(x)` inverts all bits in `x` (0s become 1s, and 1s become 0s).

Return the `k`-th bit in `S_n`. It is guaranteed that `k` is valid for the given `n`.
hints: The length of S_n is 2^n - 1. The middle bit is always '1'. If k < middle, recurse on S_{n-1}. If k > middle, look up mirrored index in S_{n-1} and invert.

title: Building Boxes
description:
You have a cubic storeroom where the walls and floor meet at 90 degrees. You are given an integer `n` representing the number of cubic boxes of equal size you have.

Boxes must touch either the floor, a wall, or be placed on top of other boxes such that each box rests entirely on another box. Return the minimum possible number of boxes touching the floor.
hints: A corner pyramid of height k contains k*(k+1)*(k+2)/6 boxes with k*(k+1)/2 touching the floor. For leftover boxes, add rows along the floor one by one.

test_cases.explanation: Place 2 boxes on the floor and 1 box on top: 2 boxes touch the floor.
Place 3 boxes on the floor in a triangle and 1 on top: 3 boxes touch the floor.

title: Count All Possible Routes
description:
You are given an array of distinct positive integers `locations` where `locations[i]` represents the position of city `i`. You are also given integers `start`, `finish`, and `fuel` representing the starting city, destination city, and initial amount of fuel you have.

At each step, if you are at city `i`, you can pick any city `j` such that `j != i` and `0 <= j < locations.length` and move to city `j`. Moving from `i` to `j` consumes `|locations[i] - locations[j]|` fuel.

Return the count of all possible routes from `start` to `finish`, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
constraints: All integers in locations are distinct.
hints: Use dynamic programming: dp(city, fuel) returns the number of valid routes from this state.

test_cases.explanation: Routes from city 1 to 3: 1->3 (5 fuel), 1->0->3 (4 fuel), 1->4->3 (3 fuel), 1->4->0->3 (5 fuel). Total = 4 routes.

title: Minimum Initial Energy to Finish Tasks
description:
You are given an array `tasks` where `tasks[i] = [actual_i, minimum_i]`:
- `actual_i` is the actual amount of energy you spend to finish the `i`-th task.
- `minimum_i` is the minimum amount of energy you require to begin the `i`-th task.

Return the minimum initial energy required to finish all the tasks.
hints: Sort tasks in descending order of (minimum_i - actual_i). Tasks with the largest saved energy buffer should be completed first.

test_cases.explanation: Starting with 8 energy: do [4, 8] (4 left), do [2, 4] (2 left), do [1, 2] (1 left). Total initial = 8.
Starting with 32 energy allows finishing all tasks.

title: Find Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges in Minimum Spanning Tree
description:
Given a weighted undirected connected graph with `n` vertices numbered from `0` to `n - 1`, and an array `edges` where `edges[i] = [from_i, to_i, weight_i]`.

A critical edge is an edge whose deletion causes the MST weight to increase or the graph to become disconnected.
A pseudo-critical edge is an edge that can appear in some MSTs but not all MSTs.

Return two lists of edge indices: `[critical_edges, pseudo_critical_edges]`.
hints: Calculate the standard MST cost with Kruskal's algorithm. An edge is critical if excluding it increases the MST cost. An edge is pseudo-critical if including it first yields an MST with the same base cost.

test_cases.explanation: Critical edges: [0, 1]. Pseudo-critical edges: [2, 3, 4, 5].
All 4 edges form a cycle with weight 1. None are critical, all 4 are pseudo-critical: [[], [0, 1, 2, 3]].

title: Count Ways to Make Array With Product
description:
You are given a 2D integer array `queries` where `queries[i] = [n_i, k_i]`.

For each query, find the number of ways to form an array of `n_i` positive integers whose product equals `k_i`.

Return an array `ans` where `ans[i]` is the answer to the `i`-th query modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: Factorize k into prime powers p^c. For each prime factor, distribute c indistinguishable prime copies among n slots using stars-and-bars: C(c + n - 1, c).

title: Count Array Pairs Divisible by K
description: Given a 0-indexed integer array `nums` of length `n` and an integer `k`, return the number of pairs `(i, j)` such that `0 <= i < j < n` and `nums[i] * nums[j]` is divisible by `k`.
hints: Replace each number with gcd(nums[i], k). The number of distinct gcd values is at most the number of divisors of k (at most 128).

test_cases.explanation: No pair product is divisible by 5. Return 0.

title: Maximum Building Height
description:
You want to build `n` new buildings in a city in a line from building 1 to `n`. Building 1 must have height 0, and adjacent buildings can differ in height by at most 1.

You are given restrictions where `restrictions[i] = [id_i, maxHeight_i]` indicates that building `id_i` must have height at most `maxHeight_i`.

Return the maximum possible height of the tallest building you can create.
hints: Propagate height restrictions forwards and backwards. Between two adjacent restricted buildings (x1, h1) and (x2, h2), the peak height is (h1 + h2 + x2 - x1) // 2.

test_cases.explanation: Heights: [0, 1, 2, 1, 2]. Maximum height is 2.
Heights: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Maximum height is 5.

title: Minimum Interval to Include Each Query
description:
You are given a 2D integer array `intervals`, where `intervals[i] = [left_i, right_i]` describes the `i`-th interval (size is `right_i - left_i + 1`). You are also given an integer array `queries`.

The answer to the `j`-th query is the size of the smallest interval `i` such that `left_i <= queries[j] <= right_i`. If no such interval exists, the answer is `-1`.

Return an array containing the answers to the queries.
hints: Sort queries and intervals. Use a min-heap to maintain active intervals ordered by length, discarding expired intervals where right < q.

title: Maximum Score Words Formed by Letters
description:
Given a list of `words`, list of single `letters` (which might be repeating) and `score` of every character.

Return the maximum score of any valid set of words formed by using the given letters (words[i] cannot be used multiple times).

It is not necessary to use all characters in `letters` and each letter can only be used once. Score of letters 'a', 'b', 'c', ..., 'z' is given by `score[0]`, `score[1]`, ..., `score[25]` respectively.
constraints: words[i], letters[i] contain only lower case English letters.
hints: Since words.length <= 14, try all 2^14 subsets of words with backtracking or bitmasking.

test_cases.explanation: Form 'dad' (score 11) and 'good' (score 12) for total score 23.
Form 'ax', 'bx', 'cx' for total score 27.

title: Max Dot Product of Two Subsequences
description:
Given two arrays `nums1` and `nums2`.

Return the maximum dot product between non-empty subsequences of `nums1` and `nums2` with the same length.

A subsequence of a array is a new array which is formed from the original array by deleting some (can be none) of the characters without disturbing the relative positions of the remaining characters.
hints: dp[i][j] is the maximum dot product using prefixes nums1[:i] and nums2[:j]. Consider taking nums1[i]*nums2[j] + max(0, dp[i-1][j-1]), skipping nums1[i], or skipping nums2[j].

title: Allocate Mailboxes
description:
Given the array `houses` where `houses[i]` is the location of the `i`-th house along a street, and an integer `k`, allocate `k` mailboxes in the street.

Return the minimum total distance between each house and its nearest mailbox.
constraints: All the integers of houses are unique.
hints: Sort houses. If 1 mailbox is placed for houses[i..j], the optimal location is the median house. Use dynamic programming to partition houses into k groups.

test_cases.explanation: Allocate mailboxes at 3, 9, 20. Total distance is |1-3| + |4-3| + |8-9| + |10-9| + |20-20| = 5.
Allocate at 3 and 14. Total distance = 9.

title: Reducing Dishes
description:
A chef has collected data on the satisfaction level of his `n` dishes. Chef can cook any dish in 1 unit of time.

Like-time coefficient of a dish is defined as the time taken to cook that dish including previous dishes multiplied by its satisfaction level: `time[i] * satisfaction[i]`.

Return the maximum sum of like-time coefficient that the chef can obtain after dishes preparation. Dishes can be prepared in any order and the chef can discard some dishes to maximize the coefficient.
hints: Sort dishes by satisfaction ascending. Greedily pick dishes from right to left as long as running sum remains positive.

test_cases.explanation: Cook dishes with satisfaction [-1, 0, 5]. Like-time coefficient = (-1)*1 + 0*2 + 5*3 = 14.
Cook all 3 dishes: 2*1 + 3*2 + 4*3 = 20.

title: Maximum Students Taking Exam
description:
Given a `m * n` matrix `seats` that represent seats in a classroom: `seats[i][j] = '#'` means broken seat, `seats[i][j] = '.'` means good seat.

Students cannot sit in broken seats, cannot sit immediately next to each other in the same row, and cannot sit diagonally in front of each other (i.e. front-left and front-right).

Return the maximum number of students that can take the exam simultaneously.
hints: Use bitmask DP: dp[row][mask] is the max students seated in rows 0..row with row having mask of students.

test_cases.explanation: We can seat at most 4 students legally in these rows.
We can seat 3 students.

title: Count the Number of Ideal Arrays
description:
You are given two integers `n` and `maxValue`, which are used to describe an ideal array.

A 0-indexed integer array `arr` of length `n` is considered ideal if:
- `1 <= arr[i] <= maxValue` for every `0 <= i < n`.
- `arr[i]` is divisible by `arr[i - 1]` for every `1 <= i < n`.

Return the number of distinct ideal arrays of length `n`, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: An array of distinct values where each divides the next has length at most 14 (since 2^14 > 10000). Count strictly increasing chains, then use stars-and-bars C(n - 1, length - 1) to distribute repetitions.

test_cases.explanation: 11 ideal arrays.

title: Longest Chunked Palindrome Decomposition
description:
You are given a string `text`. You should split it to `k` substrings `(sub_1, sub_2, ..., sub_k)` such that:
- `sub_1 + sub_2 + ... + sub_k == text`
- `sub_i == sub_{k + 1 - i}` for all `1 <= i <= k`

Return the largest possible `k`.
constraints: text consists only of lowercase English characters.
hints: Greedy matching: find the shortest non-empty prefix that equals the corresponding suffix, strip them, and recurse on the middle.

test_cases.explanation: '(ghi)(abcdef)(hello)(adam)(hello)(abcdef)(ghi)' has 7 chunks.
No matching prefix and suffix, so 1 chunk: '(merchant)'.

title: Shortest Common Supersequence
description:
Given two strings `str1` and `str2`, return the shortest string that has both `str1` and `str2` as subsequences. If there are multiple valid strings, return any of them.

A string `s` is a subsequence of string `t` if deleting some number of characters from `t` results in the string `s`.
constraints: str1 and str2 consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Find the Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) of str1 and str2, then interleave the characters of str1 and str2 around the LCS.

test_cases.explanation: 'cabac' has 'abac' and 'cab' as subsequences, and is minimal with length 5.
Identical strings give 'aaaaaaaa'.

title: Find the Closest Palindrome
description:
Given a string `n` representing an integer, return the closest integer (not including itself), which is a palindrome. If there is a tie, return the smaller one.

The closest is defined as the absolute difference minimized between two integers.
constraints: n does not have leading zeros.
n is representing an integer in the range [1, 10^18 - 1].
hints: Candidates are constructed from mirroring prefix - 1, prefix, prefix + 1, as well as 10^k - 1 and 10^k + 1.

test_cases.explanation: Closest palindrome is '121'.
Closest palindrome to 1 is '0'.

title: Build a Matrix With Conditions
description:
You are given a positive integer `k`. You are also given:
- a 2D integer array `rowConditions` of size `n` where `rowConditions[i] = [above_i, below_i]`
- a 2D integer array `colConditions` of size `m` where `colConditions[i] = [left_i, right_i]`

The numbers `1` to `k` should each appear exactly once in a `k x k` matrix, with all other cells equal to 0.

Return any matrix that satisfies the conditions. If no answer exists, return an empty matrix `[]`.
hints: Topologically sort rows and columns independently. If either graph has a cycle, return [].

test_cases.explanation: Valid topological order on rows [3, 1, 2], on columns [3, 2, 1]. Output 3x3 matrix.
Cycle in row conditions (1->2->3->1), no valid matrix exists -> [].

title: Find Building Where Alice and Bob Can Meet
description:
You are given a 0-indexed array `heights` of positive integers representing heights of buildings. You are also given `queries` where `queries[i] = [a_i, b_i]`.

Alice is at building `a_i` and Bob is at building `b_i`. Alice and Bob can move to building `j` if `a_i < j` (or `b_i < j`) and `heights[j] > heights[a_i]` and `heights[j] > heights[b_i]`. A person already at `j` stays at `j`.

Return an array `ans` where `ans[i]` is the leftmost building where they can meet, or `-1` if they cannot.
hints: If a == b or heights[b] > heights[a] (with a < b), answer is b. Otherwise, query seeks leftmost j > b with heights[j] > max(heights[a], heights[b]). Process offline with a monotonic stack.

title: Valid Arrangement of Pairs
description:
You are given a 2D integer array `pairs` where `pairs[i] = [start_i, end_i]`.

A valid arrangement of `pairs` is an arrangement such that `end_{i-1} == start_i` for all `1 <= i < pairs.length`.

Return any valid arrangement of `pairs`. It is guaranteed that a valid arrangement always exists.
constraints: A valid arrangement is guaranteed to exist.
hints: This problem asks for an Eulerian path in a directed graph. Use Hierholzer's algorithm starting from the vertex with out_degree = in_degree + 1.

title: Divide Nodes Into the Maximum Number of Groups
description:
You are given a positive integer `n` representing the number of nodes in an undirected graph, labeled from `1` to `n`. You are also given a 2D integer array `edges` where `edges[i] = [a_i, b_i]`.

Divide the nodes into `m` groups (1-indexed) such that:
- Each node belongs to exactly one group.
- For every edge `[a, b]`, if `a` is in group `x` and `b` is in group `y`, then `|x - y| == 1`.

Return the maximum number of groups `m`. If it is impossible, return `-1`.
hints: A graph can be grouped if and only if every connected component is bipartite. For each component, the max groups equals the max BFS depth starting from any node in that component.

test_cases.explanation: Nodes can be divided into 4 groups: [5], [1], [2, 4], [3, 6].
Triangle cycle (odd length) is not bipartite, return -1.

title: Making A Large Island
description:
You are given an `n x n` binary matrix `grid`. You are allowed to change at most one `0` to be `1`.

Return the size of the largest island in `grid` after applying this operation.

An island is a 4-directionally connected group of `1`s.
hints: Label each connected island of 1s with a unique ID and store its area. Then, for each 0 cell, calculate the combined area if changed to 1: 1 + sum of distinct neighbor island areas.

test_cases.explanation: Changing (0, 1) or (1, 0) connects both 1s into an island of size 3.
Changing (1, 1) gives an island of size 4.
